blocks.text: Mark 13 brings together the temple’s destruction, warnings about deception and suffering, the abomination of desolation, tribulation, Son of Man imagery, an unknown time, and the command to watch. Its many images should not be reduced to a modern prediction chart. Although many scholars commonly date Mark around 65–80 CE and relate that dating to the Jewish revolt or the temple’s destruction, the Gospel itself does not state when it was written.

The chapter’s language about the “abomination of desolation,” severe distress, the Son of Man, and judgment belongs to a wider reuse of Danielic imagery—that is, imagery associated with Daniel. The Synoptic Gospels and Revelation use such imagery in new literary settings, so these vivid scenes are part of an established scriptural pattern rather than a simple code for a single prediction.
Jesus’ instruction to watch, pray, and acknowledge that the day and hour are unknown does not authorize apocalyptic date-setting or testing God.
